indications.text: Usually viral (rhinovirus, coronavirus, influenza, adenovirus) and generally self-limited: symptomatic and supportive care only — analgesics, antipyretics, antitussives, fluids.
indications.edu: Possibly avoid antihistamines and sympathomimetics: they dehydrate bronchial secretions and may prolong symptoms.
verify: Dehydrate bronchial secretions, may prolong symptoms

indications.drug:
Doxycycline
acute bronchitis with bacteria suspected
indications.text: Routine antibiotics are not recommended (a common cause of unnecessary prescribing). With symptoms persisting more than 5 days, consider bacterial involvement: doxycycline is preferred if Mycoplasma is documented, because of macrolide resistance; macrolides (azithromycin, erythromycin, clarithromycin) are the other choice.
indications.edu: Avoid a respiratory fluoroquinolone unless there was recent antibiotic exposure: it risks resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae.
verify: Common cause for unnecessary antibiotic prescription
Persistent symptoms > 5 days, consider bacterial involvement
Preferred if mycoplasma documented due to macrolide resistance

indications.text: Outpatients do well with empiric antibiotics; diagnostic tests are not routinely performed.
indications.edu: Hospitalized patients: blood and sputum cultures before the first antibiotic. Sputum gram stain and culture are controversial: expectorated sputum is frequently contaminated and the responsible pathogen is not always identified.
verify: Patients do well with empiric ABX
Blood and sputum cultures for hospitalized patients

indications.text: First line for outpatient community-acquired pneumonia with no risk of resistant S. pneumoniae; second line: doxycycline or minocycline.
indications.edu: Outpatient pathogens: S. pneumoniae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, respiratory viruses. Current guidelines differ: they prefer amoxicillin or doxycycline for a healthy outpatient and keep a macrolide for areas where pneumococcal macrolide resistance is low.
verify: No risk of resistant S. pneumoniae
Streptococcus pneumoniae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, respiratory viruses

indications.drug:
Beta-lactam plus macrolide, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone
outpatient, resistance risk
indications.text: Risk factors for resistant S. pneumoniae: a beta-lactam plus a macrolide (amoxicillin with or without clavulanic acid; or cefuroxime or cefpodoxime, second- or third-generation cephalosporins), or a respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin).
indications.edu: The respiratory fluoroquinolone is good for patients with a beta-lactam allergy.
verify: Risk factors for resistant S. pneumoniae
Good for patients with beta-lactam allergy

indications.drug:
Penicillin-resistant S. pneumoniae
who is at risk
indications.text: Age over 65 years; a beta-lactam within the past 3 months; alcoholism; immunosuppression; medical comorbidities (diabetes, renal insufficiency, heart failure, coronary artery disease, malignancy); exposure to a child in a day care center.
indications.edu: Any one of these moves an outpatient to the broader regimen (beta-lactam plus macrolide, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone).
verify: Exposure to a child in a day care center
Risk factors for resistant S. pneumoniae

indications.drug:
Intravenous beta-lactam plus macrolide
inpatient, not in intensive care
indications.text: Intravenous beta-lactam (cefotaxime, ceftriaxone, high-dose ampicillin) plus an intravenous or oral macrolide, or plus doxycycline, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone when there is a beta-lactam allergy.
indications.edu: Ward pathogens: S. pneumoniae, M. pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, H. influenzae, Legionella, aspiration and respiratory viruses. Cultures come before the first dose.
verify: Cefotaxime, ceftriaxone, high-dose ampicillin PLUS intravenous/oral macrolide

indications.text: The same regimen as the ward, but all of it intravenous; consider MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) coverage if warranted.
indications.edu: Intensive care pathogens add S. aureus, Legionella and gram-negative bacilli to S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae.
verify: Same as above, but begin all IV treatment
S. pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, Legionella spp., Gram-negative bacilli, H. influenzae

indications.text: Lung infection not present at admission, occurring more than 48 hours after admission (hospital-acquired, ventilator-associated and health-care associated pneumonia). Start therapy as soon as possible; do not wait for a definitive culture. Start broad-spectrum antibiotics, consider multidrug-resistant pathogens, and cover MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) and Pseudomonas.
indications.edu: Streamline therapy once cultures and sensitivities are available. It is the second most common hospital infection (after urinary tract infection), commoner in the elderly and the mechanically ventilated, with higher mortality and cost.
verify: Start therapy as soon as possible
don't wait on a definitive culture
Streamline therapy once cultures and sensitivities are available
Infection of lung not present at time of admission
Second most common infection in hospitalized patients (after UTI)
Higher incidence in elderly and mechanically ventilated patients

indications.text: Pneumonia in a patient hospitalized in an acute care facility for more than 2 days in the past 90 days, living in a nursing home or long-term care facility, given recent intravenous antibiotics, chemotherapy or wound care in the previous 30 days, or on hemodialysis.
indications.edu: Current guidelines differ: the 2016 hospital-acquired pneumonia guideline dropped health-care associated pneumonia as a separate category.
verify: Hospitalized in acute care facility > 2 days in past 90 days

indications.drug:
Limited-spectrum empiric coverage
no multidrug-resistant risk factors
indications.text: Ceftriaxone (third-generation cephalosporin), or levofloxacin or moxifloxacin (choose these if atypical pathogens are a worry), or ampicillin/sulbactam, or ertapenem (narrow-spectrum carbapenem).
indications.edu: The algorithm’s NO branch: neither late onset (5 days or more) nor a risk factor for multidrug-resistant pathogens.
verify: No risk factors for MDR pathogens
Choose this group if worried about atypical pathogens

indications.drug:
Broad-spectrum empiric coverage
multidrug-resistant risk factors
indications.text: Gram-negative combination therapy: an antipseudomonal cephalosporin, carbapenem or penicillin/beta-lactamase inhibitor plus an antipseudomonal fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin, ciprofloxacin) or an aminoglycoside; plus gram-positive coverage with vancomycin or linezolid.
indications.edu: The algorithm’s YES branch: late onset (5 days or more) or risk factors — prior antibiotics, colonization, hospitalization or chronic care, immunosuppressive disease or therapy.
verify: Positive risk factors for MDR pathogens
Late onset (>=5 days) or risk factors for MDR pathogens
Prior antibiotics, colonization, hospitalization, or chronic care, immunosuppressive disease or therapy
Broad-spectrum initial antibiotic therapy for MDR pathogens

indications.drug:
Nosocomial pneumonia
after the cultures return
indications.text: Scale back antibiotic coverage as cultures become available and switch to oral therapy when possible (cheaper).
indications.edu: When therapy fails, think wrong therapy (resistant pathogens, inadequate antimicrobial therapy), wrong diagnosis (pulmonary embolus, neoplasm) or complications (C. difficile colitis, empyema, lung abscess). Duration given: 7 to 8 days, longer for P. aeruginosa and other resistant gram-negative organisms; current guidelines differ: about 7 days for most hospital-acquired pneumonia, Pseudomonas included.
verify: Scale back antibiotic coverage as cultures are available
C. difficile colitis, empyema or lung abscess

indications.group: Antipseudomonal agents, aminoglycosides, vancomycin and linezolid
indications.text: Fourth-generation cephalosporin with antipseudomonal activity, for broad-spectrum nosocomial coverage.
indications.edu: Requires renal adjustment (as does ceftazidime). The slides call ceftazidime (Fortaz) rarely used and not recommended because resistance develops rapidly; current guidelines differ: ceftazidime is still a listed antipseudomonal option.

indications.group: Antipseudomonal agents, aminoglycosides, vancomycin and linezolid
indications.text: Antipseudomonal carbapenems for broad-spectrum coverage. Ertapenem has limited activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa, so it belongs to the limited-spectrum list instead.
indications.edu: Renal adjustment for both; imipenem with caution in a seizure history, meropenem carries less seizure risk.
verify: Ertapenem has limited activity against P. aeruginosa
Use with caution in patients with seizure history

indications.group: Antipseudomonal agents, aminoglycosides, vancomycin and linezolid
indications.text: Antipseudomonal penicillin with a beta-lactamase inhibitor, for broad-spectrum coverage.
indications.edu: Requires renal adjustment. Ticarcillin/clavulanate (Timentin) is not used very often because of increased gram-negative resistance (it is no longer sold in the United States).

indications.group: Antipseudomonal agents, aminoglycosides, vancomycin and linezolid
indications.text: Antipseudomonal, with good activity against atypicals (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella) and good lung tissue penetration.
indications.edu: Increasing use is driving gram-negative resistance, so use judiciously; renal adjustment required.
verify: Increasing use leading to gram negative resistance

indications.group: Antipseudomonal agents, aminoglycosides, vancomycin and linezolid
indications.text: The gram-negative partner in broad-spectrum nosocomial coverage. Extended-interval dosing (once daily or longer): lung penetration is poor, so bigger doses give higher concentrations.
indications.edu: Adjust dose and frequency by drug levels; highly dependent on renal function; watch for ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity.
verify: Utilize extended interval dosing (once daily or longer)
Adjust dose and frequency based on levels

indications.group: Antipseudomonal agents, aminoglycosides, vancomycin and linezolid
indications.text: Primarily used for empiric MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) coverage.
indications.edu: Draw the trough before the third or fourth dose (steady state); requires renal adjustment; ototoxic, and nephrotoxic with other nephrotoxins. (The trough target is a level, not tested here; current guidelines differ: they now favor area-under-the-curve monitoring.)
verify: Primarily used for empiric MRSA coverage

indications.group: Antipseudomonal agents, aminoglycosides, vancomycin and linezolid
indications.text: Great MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) coverage, intravenous and oral forms, good lung penetration.
indications.edu: No dose adjustment for renal function; expensive.
verify: No dose adjustment based on renal function

indications.text: Two months of four drugs (isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide), then four months of isoniazid and rifampin.
indications.edu: Never single agents in active disease (resistance). Duration: pulmonary 6 to 9 months; with HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) infection 9 to 12 months; complicated disease in other body sites 18 to 24 months; isoniazid or rifampin resistance 18 to 24 months.

verify: Don't use single agents in active disease to prevent resistance development
If Isoniazid or Rifampin resistance treat 18-24 months

indications.text: Prophylaxis: used alone. Active disease: in combination.
indications.edu: Give pyridoxine (vitamin B6) to prevent the peripheral neuritis of pyridoxine deficiency. Hepatitis risk rises with alcohol use and with age.

indications.text: Primary use: tuberculosis; also meningococcal disease prophylaxis and endocarditis.
indications.edu: Rarely used alone because tolerance (resistance) develops rapidly. Warn that tears, sweat and urine turn orange. It induces liver enzymes, so check the patient’s other drugs (contraceptives, anticoagulants).
verify: Rarely used alone because of rapid tolerance

indications.text: Part of the four-drug start: the cell wall it weakens lets the other agents in.
indications.edu: 75 percent is excreted unchanged, so adjust in renal disease; resistance develops quickly if used alone; ask about vision (red-green discrimination, visual acuity).
verify: Weakened cell wall allows other agents better access
75% excreted unchanged, adjust dose in renal disease
Resistance develops quickly if used alone

indications.text: Shortens the duration of combined therapy; given for the first two months only, to avoid liver toxicity.
indications.edu: Monitor liver enzymes (hepatitis in 15 percent); every patient becomes hyperuricemic; avoid in pregnancy.
verify: Given first two months only, to avoid liver toxicity
Inhibits uric acid excretion, all hyperuricemic

indications.drug:
Second-line tuberculosis agents
resistance or intolerance
indications.text: Streptomycin, aminosalicylic acid, cycloserine, rifabutin, macrolides, quinolones, clofazimine (leprosy) and linezolid, when there is resistance or drug intolerance.
indications.edu: Not tested: know the first-line four instead. For reference, each has a signature toxicity: streptomycin auditory and vestibular; aminosalicylic acid gastrointestinal; cycloserine central nervous system (psychosis, seizures).
verify: Other agents (in case of resistance/drug intolerance)

indications.text: Endogenous catecholamine acting on alpha and beta receptors. Alpha: vasoconstriction, decreased vascular permeability. Beta: bronchial smooth muscle relaxation. Alleviates pruritus, urticaria and angioedema.
indications.edu: Intramuscular (or subcutaneous) is generally preferred unless the patient is coding (then intravenous). Two concentrations exist and they differ tenfold, so confirm which one is in hand.
verify: Acts on alpha and beta receptors
IM generally preferred unless patient is coding

indications.text: For profound vasodilation and hypotension: increases intravascular volume.
indications.edu: Severe cases need more volume. (Volumes are amounts and are not tested.)
verify: More volume will be needed for severe cases

indications.text: Massive amounts of histamine are released in acute anaphylaxis; H1 blockers relieve the rash, pruritus and hives (the cutaneous effects).
indications.edu: The H2 blocker covers what the H1 blockers do not: the systemic (vasodilation) and gastrointestinal effects.
verify: Massive amounts of histamine released during acute anaphylactic reaction

indications.text: Blocks the systemic (vasodilation) and gastrointestinal effects of histamine, such as increased gastric acid secretion.
indications.edu: Given alongside an H1 blocker, which handles the skin.

indications.text: Beta-2 agonist bronchodilator: relaxes bronchial smooth muscle.
indications.edu: Expect anxiousness, tremor and tachycardia.

indications.text: Corticosteroids block production of inflammatory mediators at the cellular level and work on all aspects of anaphylaxis.
indications.edu: They take several hours to work. Methylprednisolone is given intramuscularly or intravenously.
verify: Blocks production of inflammatory mediators at the cellular level
Works on all aspects of anaphylaxis

indications.text: Reduce bronchial responsiveness long term (it tracks airway inflammation and falls with anti-inflammatory agents such as inhaled corticosteroids) and prevent or reverse acute bronchospasm (avoid allergens and triggers; short-term beta-2 agonists).
indications.edu: Asthma is a chronic disease: long-term controllers are used daily if indicated; albuterol gives only short-term relief and should be used sparingly — excessive use means poor control and a need to adjust long-term therapy.
verify: Reduce the level of bronchial responsiveness long term
Bronchial responsiveness related to airway inflammation
Treat with short term beta-2 agonists
Long-term controller medications need to be used daily if indicated
Albuterol only provides short term relief and should be used sparingly
Excessive use indicates poor control and need for adjustment in long-term therapy

indications.drug:
Asthma medicines
quick relief or long-term control
indications.text: Quick relief: short-acting beta-2 agonists, anticholinergics, systemic corticosteroids. Long-term controllers: long-acting beta-2 agonists, inhaled corticosteroids, leukotriene modifiers, mast cell stabilizers, anti-IgE (immunoglobulin E) antibody, methylxanthines (theophylline).
indications.edu: Three approaches: reverse bronchospasm (beta-2 agonist, ipratropium, theophylline), remove the trigger (cromolyn, nedocromil), control inflammation (steroids, lipoxygenase inhibitors).

indications.drug:
Albuterol (ProAir, Ventolin), levalbuterol (Xopenex)
short-acting beta-2 agonists
indications.text: Quick relief: work rapidly and last 4 to 6 hours; raise cAMP (cyclic adenosine monophosphate) and relax airway smooth muscle.
indications.edu: Wait 15 to 30 seconds between puffs; use sparingly — frequent use is a sign of poor control.

indications.text: Long-term controllers lasting 12 hours or more.
indications.edu: Never alone for asthma: pair with an inhaled corticosteroid, as in the combination inhalers.
verify: Long acting (Do NOT use alone for asthma)

indications.text: A long-term controller of limited use, used in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; compared with long-acting bronchodilators it is less effective and less well tolerated.
indications.edu: Narrow therapeutic index: monitor plasma levels. The slides call it renally eliminated; the pharmacology differs: it is mainly metabolized by the liver, which is why rifampin’s enzyme induction lowers its levels.

indications.text: Blocks acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors, producing bronchodilation; short-acting, lasting up to 8 hours; a quick-relief medicine.
indications.edu: Warn about anticholinergic effects: dry mouth and eyes, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, tachycardia.
verify: Block acetylcholine's effect on muscarinic receptors
Dry as a bone (dry mouth, dry eyes)

indications.text: Long-acting: lasts 24 hours or more.
indications.edu: The slides disagree: the anticholinergic list marks it for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease only, while the stepwise asthma chart lists add-on tiotropium at steps 4 and 5.

indications.group: Asthma: long-term controllers and systemic steroids
indications.drug:
Inhaled corticosteroids
beclomethasone, budesonide, flunisolide, fluticasone, mometasone, triamcinolone
indications.text: Control inflammation by inhibiting the inflammatory cascade; they lower bronchial responsiveness long term.
indications.edu: Up to 8 weeks for maximal effect, so they are taken daily even when well. Watch for oral candidiasis (thrush) and, at high dose, slowed growth in children. Brands: QVAR, Pulmicort, Aerobid, Flovent, Asmanex, Azmacort.
verify: Up to 8 weeks for maximal effects
Reduced with anti-inflammatory agents (e.g. inhaled corticosteroids)

indications.group: Asthma: long-term controllers and systemic steroids
indications.text: Formoterol/budesonide (Symbicort), formoterol/mometasone (Dulera), salmeterol/fluticasone (Advair): a long-acting beta-2 agonist with an inhaled corticosteroid.
indications.edu: This is how a long-acting beta-2 agonist is used in asthma, since it is never used alone.

verify: Long acting (Do NOT use alone for asthma)

indications.group: Asthma: long-term controllers and systemic steroids
indications.text: Oral leukotriene antagonist at the leukotriene D4 receptor (cysteinyl leukotriene 1 receptor), which mediates inflammation, bronchial constriction and mucus secretion. Effective in aspirin-induced asthma.
indications.edu: A long-term controller taken by mouth. The slides call its side effects minimal; current labeling differs: it carries a FDA (Food and Drug Administration) boxed warning for serious neuropsychiatric events.
verify: receptor mediates inflammation, bronchial constriction, mucous secretion

indications.group: Asthma: long-term controllers and systemic steroids
indications.drug:
Cromolyn sodium, nedocromil (Tilade)
mast cell stabilizers
indications.text: Inhaled mast cell stabilizers that remove the trigger or antigen; limited use; mechanism unknown (may interfere with calcium).
indications.edu: Must be taken before the antigen insult, and may take up to 4 weeks to work, so they must be taken regularly.
verify: Must be taken before antigen insult
May take up to 4 weeks to work; must be taken regularly

indications.group: Asthma: long-term controllers and systemic steroids
indications.text: A recombinant humanized monoclonal antibody that binds circulating IgE (immunoglobulin E), which decreases the high-affinity receptors on mast cells and prevents degranulation.
indications.edu: Subcutaneous injection every 2 to 4 weeks. Watch for anaphylaxis; injection-site pain and bruising are expected.
verify: Binds circulating IgE which decreases high affinity receptors on mast cells, prevents degranulation

indications.group: Asthma: long-term controllers and systemic steroids
indications.drug:
Mepolizumab (Nucala), benralizumab (Fasenra), reslizumab (Cinqair), dupilumab (Dupixent)
other biologics
indications.text: For the eosinophilic phenotype (peripheral blood eosinophils above 150 per microliter). Anti-interleukin-5: mepolizumab, benralizumab, reslizumab — reslizumab is given intravenously. Anti-interleukin-4: dupilumab.
indications.edu: Side-effect profile similar to omalizumab. (Benralizumab acts on the interleukin-5 receptor.)
verify: Similar side effect profile to omalizumab (Xolair)

indications.group: Asthma: long-term controllers and systemic steroids
indications.drug:
Prednisone, prednisolone, methylprednisolone, dexamethasone
systemic corticosteroids
indications.text: Suppress, control and reverse airway inflammation and inhibit inflammatory cytokines. Most potent, but of limited use because of side effects: used in asthma exacerbations.
indications.edu: Forms: prednisone (Deltasone) oral tablet; prednisolone (Ora-Pred) oral liquid; methylprednisolone (Solu-Medrol) and dexamethasone (Decadron) oral or parenteral. A quick-relief medicine.
verify: Suppress, control, and reverse airway inflammation
Most potent but limited use due to side effects

indications.group: Inhaler devices, technique and status asthmaticus
indications.drug:
Stepwise asthma therapy
preferred controller and reliever
indications.text: Adjust treatment up and down. Preferred controller: step 1 as-needed low-dose inhaled corticosteroid-formoterol; step 2 daily low-dose inhaled corticosteroid or as-needed low-dose inhaled corticosteroid-formoterol; steps 3 to 5 low-, medium- and high-dose inhaled corticosteroid with a long-acting beta-2 agonist; step 5 adds referral for phenotypic assessment and add-on therapy (tiotropium, anti-immunoglobulin E, anti-interleukin-5 or -4 receptor).
indications.edu: Preferred reliever: as-needed low-dose inhaled corticosteroid-formoterol; other reliever: as-needed short-acting beta-2 agonist. Review inhaler technique and adherence when assessing.

indications.group: Inhaler devices, technique and status asthmaticus
indications.text: A compressor forces liquid medication into a fine mist for passive inhalation: good for children and elderly patients who cannot use a metered dose inhaler.
indications.edu: A bigger dose is given overall, so side effects may be greater; clean it regularly to prevent microbial growth.
verify: Compressor forces liquid medication into a fine mist
Allows for passive inhalation of medications
Good for children, elderly who can't use MDI
May lead to more side effects
Must be cleaned regularly to prevent microbial growth

indications.group: Inhaler devices, technique and status asthmaticus
indications.text: Medication in powder form, drawn out of the device by the patient’s own inspiratory force.
indications.edu: Not good for patients with poor inspiratory capacity; clean it regularly.
verify: Patients provide inspiratory force to draw medications out of device
Not good for patients who have poor inspiratory capacity

indications.group: Inhaler devices, technique and status asthmaticus
indications.drug:
Metered dose inhaler and spacer
device
indications.text: Liquid medication pushed out as a fine mist by a propellant in the canister; requires the most coordination of the three devices.
indications.edu: A spacer holds the medication for a patient with poor coordination. A spacer is an open tube extending the inhaler away from the mouth; a valve holding chamber has one-way valves so the patient cannot exhale into it. Both retain the large particles, leaving more small, respirable ones. Clean regularly.
verify: Propellant in canister forces medication out in a fine mist
Requires most coordination for proper use
Spacers used to hold medication for patients with poor coordination
open tube that extends the inhaler away from the patient's mouth
Have one way valves that do not allow the patient to exhale into the device
Intended to retain large particles emitted from the inhaler
Higher proportion of smaller, respirable particles

indications.group: Inhaler devices, technique and status asthmaticus
indications.text: Take off the cap and shake (prime if needed); breathe out all the way; start breathing in slowly as you press down (with a holding chamber, press first, then breathe in within 5 seconds); breathe in slowly and deeply; hold the breath for 10 seconds or as long as comfortable.
indications.edu: For quick-relief beta-2 agonists, wait 15 to 30 seconds between puffs.
verify: Start breathing in slowly as you press down on inhaler
With a holding chamber, first press down on inhaler and then begin breathing within 5 seconds
Hold your breath for 10 seconds or as long as comfortable
Take off cap and shake inhaler (may need to be primed)

indications.group: Inhaler devices, technique and status asthmaticus
indications.text: A medical emergency: an acute exacerbation that stays unresponsive to initial bronchodilator treatment. Continuous nebulized albuterol; steroids, intravenous preferred; magnesium (bolus, then continuous infusion); ketamine if intubated; aminophylline is questioned.
indications.edu: Ketamine is an NMDA (N-methyl-D-aspartate) receptor antagonist (dissociative anesthetic) that increases catecholamine release, producing bronchodilation.
verify: acute exacerbation that remains unresponsive to initial bronchodilator treatment

indications.group: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, smoking cessation and vaccines
indications.drug:
Every patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
all groups
indications.text: Chronic inflammation of the airways and lung parenchyma, generally not fully reversible, with an accelerated decline in FEV1 (forced expiratory volume in 1 second).
indications.edu: For every group: avoid risk factors such as smoking; annual influenza vaccination; pneumococcal vaccination; regular physical activity; regular review of inhaler technique; long-term oxygen if chronically hypoxemic; pulmonary rehabilitation.
verify: Avoidance of risk factor(s), such as smoking
Long-term oxygen therapy if chronic hypoxemia
Chronic inflammation of airways and lung parenchyma

indications.group: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, smoking cessation and vaccines
indications.drug:
Group A
less symptomatic, low risk
indications.text: A short-acting bronchodilator as needed: a short-acting beta-2 agonist, a short-acting muscarinic antagonist, or both.
indications.edu: Low risk = 0 or 1 exacerbation in the past year without hospitalization.
verify: Short-acting bronchodilator (SABA, SAMA, or combination of SABA-SAMA), as needed.
0 or 1 exacerbations in the past year without associated hospitalization

indications.group: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, smoking cessation and vaccines
indications.drug:
Group B
more symptomatic, low risk
indications.text: Regular long-acting bronchodilator: a long-acting muscarinic antagonist or a long-acting beta-2 agonist, chosen by patient preference.
indications.edu: A short-acting bronchodilator (usually a short-acting beta-2 agonist) for symptom relief as needed.
verify: Regular treatment with a long-acting bronchodilator, either LAMA or LABA, based on patient preference
Short-acting bronchodilator (usually SABA) for symptom relief as needed

indications.group: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, smoking cessation and vaccines
indications.drug:
Group C
less symptomatic, high risk
indications.text: Regular long-acting muscarinic antagonist; a short-acting beta-2 agonist for relief as needed.
indications.edu: High risk = 2 or more exacerbations a year, with one or more leading to hospitalization.
verify: Regular treatment with a LAMA; SABA available for symptom relief as needed.
exacerbations per year with one or more leading to hospitalization

indications.group: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, smoking cessation and vaccines
indications.drug:
Group D
more symptomatic, high risk
indications.text: Regular long-acting muscarinic antagonist, or, with severe breathlessness, a long-acting beta-2 agonist plus a long-acting muscarinic antagonist; an inhaled glucocorticoid with a long-acting beta-2 agonist may be preferred if asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease overlap.
indications.edu: A short-acting beta-2 agonist for relief as needed. Current guidelines differ: the 2023 Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease report merged groups C and D into one group E.
verify: Regular treatment with LAMA or, if severe breathlessness
Combination glucocorticoid-LABA inhaler may be preferred, if features of asthma/COPD overlap

indications.group: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, smoking cessation and vaccines
indications.text: Smoking is a major contributor: cigarette smoke is responsible for more than 85 percent of cases. Quitting can return lung function decline to the normal age-related rate and lowers lung cancer risk.
indications.edu: Combine a drug with counseling: the intensity and frequency of counseling correlate directly with success. Quitting is physical, psychological and social.
verify: Smoking - a major contributor to COPD
cigarette smoke is responsible for >85% of COPD cases
Can result in return to the normal age-related rate of decline in ventilatory function
Effective programs should combine pharmacologic intervention with counseling

indications.group: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, smoking cessation and vaccines
indications.text: Inhibits the uptake of norepinephrine and dopamine, mimicking the way nicotine indirectly activates epinephrine and dopamine in the central nervous system.
indications.edu: Avoid with a seizure disorder or with monoamine oxidase inhibitors; caution with noradrenergic antidepressants (tricyclic antidepressants, venlafaxine).
verify: inhibits the uptake of norepinephrine and dopamine

indications.group: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, smoking cessation and vaccines
indications.drug:
Nicotine replacement
patch, gum, spray, inhaler
indications.text: Reduces the craving to smoke and minimizes physical withdrawal (anxiety, irritability, restlessness, insomnia, headache, depression, nausea).
indications.edu: Therapy lasts 6 to 12 weeks, set by the level of dependence; patches and gum are over the counter; caution in cardiovascular disease (tachyarrhythmias, hypertension).
verify: Reduces craving to smoke, minimize physical withdrawal
duration of therapy is between 6-12 weeks
Patches and Gum are available OTC
Caution in patients with cardiovascular problems

indications.group: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, smoking cessation and vaccines
indications.text: Partial nicotine receptor agonist (to a lesser degree than nicotine).
indications.edu: Start one week before the quit date and continue for 12 weeks. Expect nausea, sleep disturbance and headache; the slides carry a black box warning for neuropsychiatric events (depression, suicidal ideation).
verify: partial nicotine receptor agonist (lesser degree than nicotine)
start one week before quit date and continue for 12 weeks

indications.group: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, smoking cessation and vaccines
indications.drug:
Influenza and pneumococcal vaccines
chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
indications.text: Patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease risk significant morbidity and mortality from pneumonia caused by influenza: annual influenza vaccination is highly recommended, plus the pneumococcal vaccine (Pneumovax).
indications.edu: Current guidelines differ: a pneumococcal conjugate vaccine is now the preferred pneumococcal vaccine for most adults.
verify: Patients with COPD at risk for significant morbidity and mortality from pneumonia caused by influenza
Annual influenza vaccination is highly recommended in these patients
Should also receive the pneumococcal vaccine (Pneumovax)

sideeffects.text: Dehydrate bronchial secretions; may prolong symptoms.
sideeffects.monitor: Possibly avoid them in acute bronchitis.

sideeffects.group: Antipseudomonal agents, aminoglycosides, vancomycin and linezolid
sideeffects.text: Seizures.

sideeffects.group: Antipseudomonal agents, aminoglycosides, vancomycin and linezolid

charts.title: Pneumonia and Bronchitis: Empiric Regimens by Setting
charts.sub: Acute bronchitis, community-acquired pneumonia (outpatient, ward, intensive care) and nosocomial pneumonia (limited or broad spectrum) side by side: who belongs in each setting, the likely pathogens, the empiric regimen and what to watch. No doses.

cells: Acute bronchitis
Inflammation of one or more bronchi, sparing the bronchioles and alveoli; acute at any age, chronic mainly in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

Viruses (rhinovirus, coronavirus, influenza, adenovirus); occasionally bacteria (Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, Bordetella pertussis, streptococci, staphylococci, Haemophilus), sometimes after a viral illness
Supportive care; routine antibiotics not recommended. Symptoms beyond 5 days: consider bacteria — doxycycline (preferred if Mycoplasma is documented, because of macrolide resistance) or a macrolide
Possibly avoid antihistamines and sympathomimetics; avoid a respiratory fluoroquinolone unless there was recent antibiotic exposure
verify: Preferred if mycoplasma documented due to macrolide resistance
Inflammation of one or more bronchi
Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, Bordatella pertussis

cells: Community-acquired, outpatient, no resistance risk
No risk factor for resistant S. pneumoniae
S. pneumoniae, M. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, respiratory viruses
First line: a macrolide (azithromycin, clarithromycin). Second line: doxycycline, minocycline
Empiric therapy; diagnostic tests not routinely performed. Current guidelines differ (see the note below).
verify: No risk of resistant S. pneumoniae
Streptococcus pneumoniae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis

cells: Community-acquired, outpatient, resistance risk
Age over 65, a beta-lactam in the past 3 months, alcoholism, immunosuppression, comorbidities, a child in day care at home
Penicillin-resistant S. pneumoniae on top of the outpatient list
Beta-lactam plus a macrolide (amoxicillin with or without clavulanic acid; cefuroxime or cefpodoxime) or a respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin)
The fluoroquinolone route suits a beta-lactam allergy
verify: Risk factors for resistant S. pneumoniae
Good for patients with beta-lactam allergy
Exposure to a child in a day care center

cells: Community-acquired, inpatient (not intensive care)
Admitted to the ward
S. pneumoniae, M. pneumoniae, C. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, Legionella, aspiration, respiratory viruses
Intravenous beta-lactam (cefotaxime, ceftriaxone, high-dose ampicillin) plus an intravenous or oral macrolide, or doxycycline, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone (beta-lactam allergy)
Blood and sputum cultures before antibiotics; sputum gram stain is controversial (often contaminated)
verify: Cefotaxime, ceftriaxone, high-dose ampicillin PLUS intravenous/oral macrolide
Blood and sputum cultures for hospitalized patients

cells: Community-acquired, intensive care
Admitted to the intensive care unit
S. pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, Legionella, gram-negative bacilli, H. influenzae
Same as the ward, all intravenous
Consider MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) coverage if warranted
verify: Same as above, but begin all IV treatment
Staphylococcus aureus, Legionella spp., Gram-negative bacilli

cells: Nosocomial, limited spectrum
Pneumonia more than 48 hours after admission, with neither late onset (5 days or more) nor a multidrug-resistant risk factor
Nosocomial pathogens without multidrug resistance; levofloxacin or moxifloxacin if atypical pathogens are a worry
Ceftriaxone, or levofloxacin or moxifloxacin, or ampicillin/sulbactam, or ertapenem
Start at once; streamline when cultures and sensitivities return
verify: No risk factors for MDR pathogens

cells: Nosocomial, broad spectrum
Late onset (5 days or more) or a multidrug-resistant risk factor: prior antibiotics, colonization, hospitalization or chronic care, immunosuppressive disease or therapy

Gram-negative bacilli (Pseudomonas aeruginosa most common, E. coli, K. pneumoniae, Acinetobacter, Enterobacter, Serratia); gram-positive cocci (MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) most common, S. pneumoniae); fungi (Candida, Aspergillus fumigatus)
Antipseudomonal cephalosporin, carbapenem or penicillin/beta-lactamase inhibitor PLUS an antipseudomonal fluoroquinolone or an aminoglycoside, PLUS vancomycin or linezolid
Must cover MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) and Pseudomonas; do not wait for a definitive culture
verify: Positive risk factors for MDR pathogens
Late onset (>=5 days) or risk factors for MDR pathogens

cells: Nosocomial, after cultures
Cultures and sensitivities are back
The organism grown
Scale back coverage; switch to oral therapy when possible (cheaper)
If it fails: wrong therapy, wrong diagnosis (pulmonary embolus, neoplasm) or a complication (C. difficile colitis, empyema, lung abscess)
verify: Scale back antibiotic coverage as cultures are available

charts.notes: Read the regimen column as a ladder. Outpatient pneumonia with no resistance risk gets one drug; a resistance risk adds a beta-lactam to the macrolide (or swaps both for a respiratory fluoroquinolone, the beta-lactam allergy route); the ward makes the beta-lactam intravenous; intensive care makes everything intravenous and adds thought about methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. In the hospital, the question is whether multidrug-resistant risk is present: no gives one limited-spectrum drug, yes gives three (two gram-negative drugs plus vancomycin or linezolid). Current guidelines differ on two points: they prefer amoxicillin or doxycycline over a macrolide for a healthy outpatient (macrolides only where pneumococcal resistance is low), and the 2016 hospital-acquired pneumonia guideline no longer uses health-care associated pneumonia as a category. The slides are what you are tested on. Doses are not tested and are left out.

charts.title: Tuberculosis Drugs Compared
charts.sub: The four first-line drugs and the second-line agents: whether each is bacteriostatic or bactericidal, what it targets, how it is used, its signature adverse effects, what to monitor and teach, and how it is eliminated or resisted. No doses.

cells: The regimen
—
Mycobacteria are acid-fast bacilli with a waxy mycolic acid coat; M. tuberculosis grows very slowly and can lie dormant, so drugs that act on cell division work less well

Two months of isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol and pyrazinamide, then four months of isoniazid and rifampin; pulmonary 6 to 9 months, with HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) 9 to 12, complicated 18 to 24
—
Never single agents in active disease
Isoniazid or rifampin resistance: treat 18 to 24 months

verify: very slow growing, can exist in dormant states for long periods of time
Don't use single agents in active disease to prevent resistance development
If Isoniazid or Rifampin resistance treat 18-24 months

cells: Isoniazid
Bacteriostatic for latent, bactericidal for dividing bacteria
Inhibits mycolic acid production (the waxy cell coat); activated by the bacterial catalase-peroxidase
Prophylaxis alone; active disease in combination
Peripheral neuritis (pyridoxine deficiency); hepatitis (more in alcoholics and with age); lupus-like syndrome; seizures, euphoria, psychosis, memory impairment
Give pyridoxine (vitamin B6); liver tests, especially with alcohol use or older age
75 to 95 percent excreted as an acetylated metabolite (fast and slow acetylators); well absorbed, enters the central nervous system; resistance by mutation in the activating enzyme’s gene

verify: Resistance by mutation in DNA coding for activation enzyme

cells: Rifampin
Not stated
Inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase by forming a complex with the enzyme (no effect on the human enzyme); a semi-synthetic rifamycin
Tuberculosis; meningococcal disease prophylaxis; endocarditis
Orange tears, sweat and urine; induces cytochrome P450 enzymes; jaundice, hepatitis; flu-like hypersensitivity (20 percent); gastrointestinal upset
Warn about the orange color; review interacting drugs (anticoagulants, contraceptives, digoxin, ketoconazole, theophylline)
Rarely used alone: tolerance develops rapidly
verify: Rarely used alone because of rapid tolerance

cells: Ethambutol
Bacteriostatic
Mechanism unknown: inhibits mycolic acid incorporation into membranes; no effect on other bacteria; the weakened cell wall lets the other agents in
First two months of the four-drug start
Visual disturbances: decreased red-green discrimination and visual acuity; increased uric acid
Ask about vision and color perception
75 percent excreted unchanged: adjust in renal disease; resistance develops quickly if used alone
verify: inhibits mycolic acid incorporation into membranes
Weakened cell wall allows other agents better access
75% excreted unchanged, adjust dose in renal disease

cells: Pyrazinamide
Not stated
Converted to pyrazinoic acid, which lowers the pH so the bacteria cannot grow; enters macrophages; exact target unclear
Shortens the combined course; given in the first two months only
Hepatitis (15 percent); hyperuricemia in every patient (inhibits uric acid excretion)
Monitor liver enzymes; avoid in pregnancy
Limited to the first two months to avoid liver toxicity
verify: lowers pH so bacteria can't grow, enters macrophages

cells: Second-line agents
—
—
Resistance or drug intolerance: streptomycin, aminosalicylic acid, cycloserine, rifabutin, macrolides, quinolones, clofazimine (leprosy), linezolid
Streptomycin auditory and vestibular; aminosalicylic acid gastrointestinal; cycloserine central nervous system (psychosis, seizures)
Hearing and balance; stomach upset; mood and seizures
—
verify: Other agents (in case of resistance/drug intolerance)

charts.notes: One signature per drug. Isoniazid: peripheral neuritis, prevented by pyridoxine. Rifampin: orange secretions and enzyme induction (it lowers contraceptives and anticoagulants). Ethambutol: red-green color vision. Pyrazinamide: hyperuricemia and hepatitis, and not in pregnancy. Three of the four can inflame the liver (isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide). Isoniazid and ethambutol both act on the waxy mycolic acid coat; rifampin acts on RNA polymerase. The slides disagree with standard microbiology on one point: rifampin’s spectrum list puts Neisseria and Legionella among gram-positive organisms; both are gram-negative, and the list is not used here. Doses are not tested and are left out.

charts.title: Asthma and Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease Drugs Compared by Class
charts.sub: Every respiratory drug class side by side: quick relief or long-term controller, how it works, what it causes and what to teach. Smoking cessation agents are at the end. No doses.

cells:
Short-acting beta-2 agonists
albuterol (ProAir, Ventolin), levalbuterol (Xopenex)
Quick relief; work rapidly, last 4 to 6 hours

cells:

formoterol (Foradil), salmeterol (Serevent)
Controller; last 12 hours or more

Never alone for asthma: only with an inhaled corticosteroid

cells:

beclomethasone, budesonide, flunisolide, fluticasone, mometasone, triamcinolone
Controller
Inhibit the inflammatory cascade; lower bronchial responsiveness long term

Combination inhalers
Symbicort, Dulera, Advair
Controller
Formoterol/budesonide (Symbicort), formoterol/mometasone (Dulera), salmeterol/fluticasone (Advair): a long-acting beta-2 agonist plus an inhaled corticosteroid

charts.notes: Read the second column first. The quick-relief drugs are the short-acting beta-2 agonists, the anticholinergics and the systemic corticosteroids; everything else is a long-term controller taken daily whether or not the patient feels well. Two never-alone rules: a long-acting beta-2 agonist is never used alone in asthma (hence the combination inhalers), and the mast cell stabilizers must be taken before the exposure. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease by group (slide 102): group A a short-acting bronchodilator as needed; group B a long-acting muscarinic antagonist or long-acting beta-2 agonist; group C a long-acting muscarinic antagonist; group D a long-acting muscarinic antagonist, or both long-acting bronchodilators with severe breathlessness, or an inhaled glucocorticoid with a long-acting beta-2 agonist when asthma overlaps; every group avoids smoking and gets influenza and pneumococcal vaccines. Current guidelines differ: the 2023 report merged groups C and D into group E. Doses are not tested and are left out.
